M11_S01.summary: The thirteen ethically variable factors fall into seven universals and six occasionals; the occasionals arise only in some cittas and take their moral quality from the citta they accompany.
body: The ethically variable factors (Aññasamāna) — literally 'common to the other' — fall into two groups: the seven universals (Sabbacittasādhāraṇa), already studied, and the six occasionals (Pakiṇṇaka), the subject of this module.

They are called 'occasional' because these six are present only in SOME cittas, scattered unevenly through the classes of consciousness. In this they differ sharply from the universals, which are present in every citta without exception.
The six occasional factors are: initial application (Vitakka), sustained application (Vicāra), decision (Adhimokkha), energy (Vīriya), rapture (Pīti) and desire-to-act (Chanda).

Because they belong to the ethically variable class, none of the six is wholesome or unwholesome in itself. When the accompanying citta is wholesome they become wholesome; when it is unwholesome they become unwholesome.

M11_S02.summary: Initial application throws the mind onto the object and sustained application keeps it pressed there — the bee flying to the lotus and the bee circling it — and neither is present in the ten sense consciousnesses.
body: Vitakka comes from 'vi' (special, particular) and the root 'takk' (to think, to consider, to form a notion). Initial application is therefore thinking of a special kind: the mind's first movement towards its object.
Its chief characteristic is to lift the co-arisen mental factors up to the object and to place them upon it — as if throwing the associated factors onto the object so that they land there.

The fourfold definition of initial application: characteristic — leading the co-arisen states to the object; function — making consciousness and its factors touch the object; manifestation — the meeting of consciousness and its factors with the object; proximate cause — the object itself together with the other three mental aggregates.

Vicāra comes from 'vi' (special) and 'car' (to roam, to move about freely). Sustained application examines the object, moving around it, keeping consciousness pressed continuously upon it and investigating it closely.

The traditional similes mark the difference: initial application is like a bee flying straight to a lotus, like a bird beating its wings to take off, like the striking of a drum; sustained application is like the bee circling the lotus to inspect it, like the bird gliding on outstretched wings, like the drum's lingering resonance.

Initial and sustained application are absent from the five pairs of sense consciousnesses (the ten cittas of eye-, ear-, nose-, tongue- and body-consciousness), because those cittas work purely mechanically through the impact of the object and require no thinking at all.

M11_S03.summary: Decision releases the mind from wavering and settles it on the object; it is absent from the ten sense consciousnesses and from the citta of doubt, and so arises in 110 cittas.
body: Adhimokkha comes from 'adhi' together with the root 'muc' (to release). Decision releases the mind from DOUBT so that it can advance upon the object; it is resolve, conviction, settled judgement.

The fourfold definition of decision: characteristic — deciding, and so breaking up the state of wavering; function — making consciousness certain about the object, without hesitation; manifestation — a judgement already reached about the object; proximate cause — an object that has to be weighed and decided upon.
Judgement is of two kinds: wrong decision, which takes what is right to be wrong and what is wrong to be right; and right decision, which takes what is right as right and what is wrong as wrong.

Decision is absent from the five pairs of sense consciousnesses (ten cittas) and from the delusion-rooted citta associated with doubt — eleven in all. It therefore arises in 110 cittas (121 minus 11).

M11_S04.summary: Energy supports the co-arisen states so that they do not fall away; its wholesome form is the Four Right Strivings, and it functions as faculty, power, enlightenment factor and path factor.
body: Vīriya derives from 'vīra', one who strives energetically. Energy is exertion, effort, support and upholding — diligence, perseverance and the capacity to endure.

The fourfold definition of energy: characteristic — the mode of exerting and enduring; function — supporting the co-arisen states so that they do not fall back; manifestation — not collapsing, not retreating; proximate cause — a sense of urgency, something that stirs the mind such as the sight of ageing, sickness, death or suffering.

Energy is of two kinds: wrong effort, diligence applied to what is unwholesome — being industrious in cheating and deceit, for example — and right effort, which is set out as the Four Right Strivings.

The Four Right Strivings are: guarding effort, so that unarisen evil states do not arise, through carefulness and mindfulness; abandoning effort, striving to destroy evil states that have already arisen; developing effort, striving to bring about wholesome states not yet arisen; and maintaining effort, preserving and strengthening wholesome states already arisen.

Energy shows four aspects according to its role: the faculty of energy, which governs and directs; the power of energy, unshakeable in the face of opposing states; energy as an enlightenment factor, the exertion that leads to awakening; and right effort as a path factor, the active destruction of the kamma that sustains the round, culminating in Nibbāna.

M11_S05.summary: Rapture has five grades and three moral natures, and desire-to-act has three kinds; desire is missing from the two delusion-rooted cittas and the eighteen rootless cittas.
body: Pīti comes from 'pī' — to be glad, to delight. Rapture is gladness, delight, keen interest, elation, exhilaration, refreshment and satisfaction in the object.

Rapture is of five grades: minor rapture, a slight thrill that raises the hairs of the body and quickly passes; momentary rapture, flashing like lightning; showering rapture, breaking over the body in waves like the tide; uplifting rapture, so buoyant that the body feels as if it would rise into the air; and pervading rapture, a full, saturating delight that suffuses the whole body and lasts.

By moral nature rapture is of three kinds: wholesome rapture, delighting in another's happiness, in meritorious deeds and as a factor of jhāna; unwholesome rapture, delight and relish in sense pleasures or in defeating an enemy; and indeterminate rapture, the joy of the Arahants.
Chanda comes from the root 'chad' — to wish, to desire. Desire-to-act is simply the wish to do, as yet uncoloured by the wholesome, the unwholesome or the indeterminate.

Desire is of three kinds: craving desire, the thirst that seeks after the six sense objects — one of the five hindrances, and unwholesome; desire for the Dhamma, the rightful wish that is the basis for success (chanda-iddhipāda), the wish to perform wholesome deeds such as giving, meditation and virtue; and functional desire, the wish to act of Arahants, who live by functional consciousness alone.

Desire is absent from the two delusion-rooted cittas (associated with doubt and with restlessness) and from the eighteen rootless cittas: these work mechanically through the impact of base and object, with no wish to do anything at all.

M2_S01.summary: Of the fourteen unwholesome mental factors, the four of the delusion group are the unwholesome universals, present in every one of the twelve unwholesome cittas.
body: The unwholesome mental factors (Akusala cetasika) are fourteen in number, and are studied in groups led by the delusion group.

Akusala — the unwholesome — carries five senses: (1) diseased, bringing suffering; (2) not lovely, bad, defiled; (3) unskilful, with reason clouded by greed, hatred and delusion; (4) faulty, blameworthy; (5) productive of painful results.
The delusion group (Mocatuka cetasika) comprises four factors: delusion (Moha), shamelessness (Ahirika), fearlessness of wrongdoing (Anottappa) and restlessness (Uddhacca).

These four are called the unwholesome universals because all four are present in every unwholesome citta. They open the way and lead the other unwholesome factors, and they are found together in all twelve unwholesome cittas.

M2_S02.summary: Shamelessness feels no shame at evil and fearlessness of wrongdoing no dread of it; the two always arise together and are the direct opposites of moral shame and moral dread.
body: Shamelessness (Ahirika) is the state of feeling no shame before what is evil, of not being ashamed to commit a fault.
Fearlessness of wrongdoing (Anottappa) is the state of having no dread, no hesitation before the consequences of an evil deed.
The source stresses that shamelessness and fearlessness of wrongdoing always travel together: wherever there is no hesitation and no shame, both factors are present at once.

They are the exact opposites of moral shame (Hiri) and moral dread (Ottappa) in the group of beautiful universals, which are called the guardians of the world precisely because they restrain what these two let loose.

M2_S03.summary: Restlessness is the agitation that will not settle on an object; it accompanies all twelve unwholesome cittas and is the hindrance opposed to the jhāna factor of happiness.
body: Uddhacca is made up of 'u' (up, above) and the root 'dhu' (to shake, to tremble). Restlessness is a shaking on the surface of the mind: unsteadiness, flickering, agitation, distraction, want of composure.

The source offers a series of images: a horse's hoof that leaves the ground the instant it touches it and strikes elsewhere; a fish lifted out of the water, thrashing about; a mind that has just taken an object and is immediately dragged off to another; clouds that gather and are at once scattered by the wind; dust blown in all directions.

Points to remember: restlessness is present in all twelve unwholesome cittas; it is associated with the four mental aggregates; it is not associated with the aggregate of materiality; it is of unwholesome class and shares the unwholesome nature.
Restlessness is also one of the five hindrances, and as a hindrance it is the opponent of the jhāna factor of happiness (sukha), which is why a scattered mind cannot settle into absorption.

M12_S01.summary: A rootless citta arises without any of the six roots accompanying it, though it still stands on past kamma as a root of another time; the eighteen divide into fifteen resultants and three functionals.
body: A rootless citta (Ahetuka Citta) is a consciousness which, at the moment it arises, has within itself no root arising together with it.
The roots are six: the unwholesome roots greed, hatred and delusion, and the wholesome roots non-greed, non-hatred and non-delusion. A rootless citta is one in which none of these six is co-arisen.

Although no root is present now, a rootless citta still rests upon a root in the past — a root of another time (nānākālika hetu). Such a citta is a result brought to maturity by wholesome or unwholesome kamma performed earlier.

The eighteen rootless cittas fall into two classes: fifteen rootless resultants (Ahetuka Vipāka) — seven unwholesome-resultant and eight wholesome-resultant — and three rootless functionals (Ahetuka Kiriyā).

M12_S02.summary: The seven unwholesome-resultant rootless cittas are the bare results of past unwholesome kamma: five sense consciousnesses (body-consciousness accompanied by pain), receiving and investigating.
body: The unwholesome-resultant rootless cittas (Ahetuka Akusala Vipāka) are the results brought to maturity by unwholesome causes in the past — killing, stealing, sexual misconduct and the like. They are seven in number.

Five of them are sense consciousnesses: eye-, ear-, nose- and tongue-consciousness, each accompanied by equanimity; and body-consciousness accompanied by PAIN — the knowing that depends on the body-sensitivity and must receive an undesirable, painful object.
The sixth is receiving consciousness accompanied by equanimity (Sampaṭicchana), which takes up from the sense consciousness the object that has come in from outside.
The seventh is investigating consciousness accompanied by equanimity (Santīraṇa), whose task is to examine and look into the object just received.

M12_S03.summary: The eight wholesome-resultant rootless cittas mirror the seven, except that body-consciousness here is accompanied by pleasure and investigating occurs both with equanimity and with joy.
body: The wholesome-resultant rootless cittas (Ahetuka Kusala Vipāka) are the results produced by wholesome causes in the past. They are eight in number.

Five are sense consciousnesses: eye-, ear-, nose- and tongue-consciousness, each accompanied by equanimity; and body-consciousness accompanied by PLEASURE, since the object met at the body-door is a desirable one.
The sixth is receiving consciousness accompanied by equanimity, resultant of wholesome kamma, which takes up the object from the sense consciousness.

The last two are investigating consciousnesses: one accompanied by equanimity, and one accompanied by joy (Somanassa-sahagataṃ Santīraṇa), which arises when the object is exceptionally desirable — the only rootless citta with joyful feeling besides the smile-producing citta.

M12_S04.summary: The three rootless functionals — five-door adverting, mind-door adverting and the Arahant's smile-producing citta — merely perform their task and create no kamma.
body: The rootless functional cittas (Ahetuka Kiriyā) are three: five-door adverting, mind-door adverting, and the smile-producing consciousness accompanied by joy.

Five-door adverting (Upekkhāsahagataṃ Pañcadvārāvajjana), accompanied by equanimity: when a visible form enters the eye and strikes the stream of consciousness, the life-continuum vibrates, and this citta arises turning the mind towards the eye-door before passing away so that eye-consciousness can arise. It depends on the heart-base and does not occur in the immaterial realms.

Mind-door adverting (Upekkhāsahagataṃ Manodvārāvajjana), accompanied by equanimity: its task is to determine the object that has come in from outside, and in a mind-door process it opens the way for the impulsions that will create kamma.
The smile-producing consciousness (Hasituppāda), accompanied by joy, is the functional citta by which an Arahant smiles. Being merely functional, it creates no kamma and yields no result.
